active_trends.text: Removal of climate from security vehicles rather than only from language — and this week the milder form, which may be the more durable one. A parliamentary defence committee reporting on the Arctic on 22 October makes warming the premise of the whole strategic problem, without hedging, and then recommends frigates, towed arrays and under-ice submarines. The referent was not removed; it was demoted to scene-setting. Against that, a national government stood up a standing climate-security taskforce with the referent in its title on 21 October, which is the first move this trend has had running the other way since it was opened. The trend now has two forms to distinguish: deletion from instruments that bind, and demotion to premise in instruments that buy.

Closed this week, as last week said it should be, and replaced by the trend below. The finding it recorded held for ten weeks and is now complete: American adaptation survives federally only as emergency management, and the week's only federal act touching the hazard was a disaster declaration for Guam. What has displaced the reframing is no longer in doubt either — the institute's new programme line is artificial intelligence and its director has taken a seat in another country's government process. The question of where the capacity goes is a better question than the question of what it is called, so it gets its own trend.

Security Council shift from climate security to natural resource governance, and now past it — and this week the month closed and the destination is legible. The October programme carried no climate, water, food-security or environment item in any framing. The last available route, the joint seminar with the African Union on 22 October, took natural resources as "illegal exploitation ... as a factor that exacerbates armed conflicts in Africa", co-led by the United States and China. The African council had proposed resource *management*; Russia proposed *root causes*; European members resisted the Russian text and the narrowest formulation won. So the trajectory is complete: climate security, then resource governance, then resource crime. Each step narrows what the Council can be asked to consider while keeping the word "resources" on the agenda, and the last step moves the subject from how states allocate to who steals — which is, as this week's curriculum reading argues at length, a description of a symptom doing duty as a theory of a cause.

Retreat from binding multilateral environmental instruments, and the thing that binds them to reality is now nine days into a deadlock with no scheduled next attempt. The panel's sixty-fifth plenary remains suspended with the assessment timetable and the 2027 budget both open and no date set, against a requirement to reconvene before the year ends to adopt a budget at all. Nobody has proposed leaving anything. Add this week's variant: a flagship report conceding that the limit the whole architecture was built around will be exceeded, which loosens every instrument that cites that limit without amending any of them.

Dutch institutional creation with fiscal non-commitment, and this week the pattern inverted in a way worth recording. The 5 million euro structural defence line stands and its action plan is now three months and three weeks overdue; no cabinet response on water at a sixth checkpoint; the parliamentary motion asking for a first national briefing on climate, nature and security during 2026 has nine weeks left. What is new is that Dutch capability is visibly in demand abroad: the director-general of the national meteorological institute sits on the British taskforce whose membership was published on 21 October. So the country supplies the expertise to another state's standing body while having no standing body of its own. That is not absence of capacity; it is absence of a domestic vehicle to put it in, which is the same pattern this trend has tracked in money, one level up.

The assets a changing hazard environment destroys are increasingly publicly indispensable, and this week produced the first number on the other side of the ledger. The loss and damage fund set aside 20 million dollars against a 4.8 billion dollar recovery estimate, which is four tenths of one per cent, and 20 million is its ceiling for any single project. Nothing in the decision addresses the privately held share of the loss. Meanwhile the week's other lesson came from Guam, where the two military installations kept their power and about half the civilian island did not: the indispensable asset was defended and the society around it was not, by the same government, in the same storm.

The climate referent and the security register being decoupled by venue — and this week the cleanest instance yet, in one country. On 21 October a British department published a standing taskforce whose title is national security and resilience risks of a changing climate and nature loss. On 22 October a British parliamentary committee published an Arctic defence report in which warming is the premise and the recommendations are hulls and sonar. Same state, same week, two registers: where the subject is risk the vocabulary is free, and where the subject is capability it is absent. The decoupling is no longer between institutions or between documents. It is between what a document is for.

The contest is moving from the hazard to the apparatus that measures and prices it, and this week the apparatus produced the week's two defining numbers and both exceeded their own instruments. The meteorological agency projected a tropical Pacific anomaly of up to 3.8°C and said that is off the monitoring charts it has used for forty years. The environment programme published a best case of a 1.7-to-1.8°C mid-century peak, which is above the limit its own convention is organised around. And the climate panel, which certifies what governments may call best available science, cannot say when its next assessment arrives or how next year is paid for. Three measurement institutions, three statements that their own reference frame no longer fits, in one week.

Forecast quality and institutional calendars have come apart, and this week the gap acquired a price and a name. The price: a projection of 874,319 people displaced in Somalia between October and December against a preparedness appeal 14.4 per cent funded, and more than 50 million dollars released from the global emergency fund for eleven front-line countries against 50 million people said to face increased hunger — about a dollar a head. The name came from the field's own literature on 22 October: who owns the gap between the forecast and the money? Forecasting agencies sit in one part of government and early-action money in another; humanitarian aid moves after disasters, development budgets are planned years ahead, and defence budgets are aimed at other threats. The mismatch is no longer this digest's observation. It is the stated position of the director of the field's best-known peace-research programme on climate.

The evidentiary question for climate loss is shifting from attribution to foreseeability, and this week the first institution that had to decide something decided it without reference to either. The loss and damage fund allocated money for the Himalayan cascade on 22 October. No public account of its reasoning mentions the hazard-environment attribution of 17 September or the forty-eight-day precursor signal published on 13 October, and no account of the decision text records any standard of evidence for a claim from an unattributed event. That is not the question being resolved; it is the question being kept open, and the mechanism is the one in D4 — a window declared Nepal-only needs no standard, because there is no route for a standard to govern. Watch for the secretariat's lessons assessment, which the board did commission, because that is where a standard would first have to be written down.

Where displaced climate-security capacity goes. Opened this week as the successor to the disaster-operations trend, and it opens with an answer rather than a question. The director of the American climate-security institute — formerly the deputy director of the strategic futures group at the national intelligence council, founding chair of a congressionally mandated climate security advisory council — took a seat on a British government's new standing taskforce, announced 23 October. Her institute's state-level briefing series stopped on 18 September; its parent's new programme line is artificial intelligence and national security. On the same British taskforce: the head of a German institute's climate diplomacy and security programme, and the director-general of the Dutch national meteorological institute. So the capacity is not evaporating, it is relocating, and the destination is a national government that is not the one that trained most of it. Three things to track. Whether any other American principal in this field takes a foreign public appointment. Whether the British taskforce's recommendations ever reach a spending document, because an advisory seat with no budget is a holding pattern rather than a destination. And whether the institutes that lose their principals to it keep publishing.

open_threads.text: The Dutch institute's current funding phase. Unmoved, and the route has now failed for a seventh consecutive week: the institute's own domain refused retrieval again. The last publicly datable announcement of a funding phase for the platform remains December 2019. What the separately hosted feed carried this week were two items by other institutions — a commentary on climate and Indian warfare on 19 October and an American institute's Gulf energy infrastructure report on 23 October — so it answers a question about curation, not about the institute. Seven refusals is a statement about one route; the thing that would settle this is a funding document from any host at all, and none has been found.

Whether the alliance published a fourth Climate Change and Security Impact Assessment. Still no, still no statement, and this week the displacing activity produced its own silence. The alliance's climate centre held its invitation-only Montréal summit on 15 and 16 October and neither it nor its Canadian co-host has published anything about it ten days on, against recaps within days of both previous editions and, for the 2025 edition, a Canadian defence minister's speech published on his own government's site. So the annual public judgement has not resumed and the room that replaced it does not report either. Two instruments, both opaque.

Whether the International Military Council's World Climate and Security Report has formally lapsed. Eighth consecutive week of silence. Its secretary general was on the Montréal speaker list and nothing has been published from that meeting, so the council's activity and its silence are now the same fact: it is in the room and not in print. No statement about the report series has ever been made.
Funding trajectory of the joint United Nations climate security unit.
open_threads.resolution: Answered in magnitude, by a printed portfolio report rather than by the dashboard that has refused to render for three weeks. Cumulative deposits to the joint programme between 2016 and 2024 were $18.27 million, which places it thirteenth of fifteen funds in the trust fund office's climate and environment portfolio, against $808.89 million for the largest and about $2 million a year for this one. Fourteen governments contribute, eleven of them European; the Netherlands is not among them. The programme is not being wound down — a third phase runs 2026 to 2028 with ten advisers deployed — and it is funded at the level of a mid-sized national research grant. One consequence for this digest's own published record: Britain's £1 million of 25 September, reported here as three tenths of one per cent of a £331 million package and treated as a rounding error, is on the order of 5 per cent of everything this programme has ever received. The denominator was wrong. What remains unanswered is the year-by-year trajectory and whether the third phase has a stated requirement, which is carried forward as a separate question.

open_threads.text: Whether the 2028-2034 Union budget carries a security-tagged climate line. Not advanced internally, and the external deadline is now two days away: the Commission's climate resilience package is reported for 28 October, and reporting of its pre-briefing says there is no ring-fenced money in it, with adaptation tied instead to the long-term budget negotiation. If that is right, the resilience framework and the budget line become the same question, and the answer is deferred to a negotiation about everything.

Chinese defence doctrine on climate. Tenth week of nothing, and the instrument was retired last week in favour of the venues where China actually acts. One of those produced something this week: China co-led, with the United States, the illegal-exploitation-of-natural-resources item at the two Councils' joint seminar on 22 October. That is a Chinese willingness to discuss resources and armed conflict in a Security Council format, on a framing that locates the problem in criminal extraction rather than in governance, scarcity or climate — consistent with the position China has held since 2007 and the first positive observable on this file in ten weeks. The other venue, the bilateral river mechanism, produced nothing for a fourth week and its flood-season window has now closed.

Any Indian security document on climate. Tenth week of nothing, and the useful finding this week is about the denominator rather than the document. A study published on 1 October, covering 8,702 parliamentary questions from December 2015 to December 2025, puts climate topics at 3.3 per cent of them. The document this digest keeps failing to find is not being withheld; by that measure the subject is barely raised in the legislature at all. The three instruments that do carry the file stand: the treaty expiry on 12 December, the river mechanism with China, and the Delhi institute's argument about why South Asian climate cooperation does not happen. The parliamentary committees were reconstituted with effect from 26 September, so the committee route now exists and is empty.
Swiss Re sigma citation for the $424bn 2025 protection gap.
open_threads.resolution: The citation is **sigma 1/2026**, *Natural catastrophes in 2025: the persistent rise of wildfire and storm risk*, Swiss Re Institute. The protection gap of $424 billion for 2025, up from $395 billion in 2024, with the natural catastrophe resilience index broadly stable at 27.3 per cent, comes from the Institute's Natural Catastrophe Insurance Resilience Index and is expressed in premium-equivalent terms. Caveat on strength: the reinsurer's own page would not open and the mirrored PDF's text could not be extracted, so the figures are corroborated across Swiss Re's own social post and several independent trade reports rather than read off the document.

open_threads.text: Whether any event attribution study of the 26 August Langtang-Lirung cascade appears.
open_threads.resolution: Resolved on 17 September 2026, and the answer is not one of the two the thread was framed to expect. World Weather Attribution published *Rapid Warming in the Himalaya Exacerbates Geohazard Cascades Beyond Adaptation Limits*, with contributors in ten countries across glaciology, mountain hydrology, climate science, seismology, humanitarian practice and social science. It attributes the hazard environment and not the event: about 1.5°C added to July-August temperatures by human-caused climate change, about 2°C annually — larger than global mean warming — individual winter months as much as 3°C, and the 0°C isotherm rising roughly 100 metres a decade into the bedrock that failed. It states explicitly that it has not assessed whether this specific rock-ice avalanche would have occurred without human-induced climate change, while asserting that warming at a rate beyond the global mean increases the likelihood and severity of such hazards. It then concludes that the event exceeded the design and predictive limits of existing risk reduction, that no existing early warning system could have provided sufficient lead time, that this constitutes a soft limit to adaptation given constrained habitable land and population increase, and that addressing loss and damage through recovery and reconstruction has become an unavoidable part of climate response. So: no event attribution, a hazard-environment attribution, and the policy conclusion reached through adaptation limits instead of causation. The successor question is the `adaptation-limits-adjudication` thread. Reporting figures that travelled with it: the debris flood ran 200 km in under seven hours at average speeds around 188 km/h and deposited 30.5 million cubic metres of material.

open_threads.text: What the HiRISK consortium is: membership, funding, institutional home.
open_threads.resolution: Resolved from hirisk.org, which was opened and read. HiRISK describes itself as 'a loose consortium of experts from High Mountain Asia and beyond', producing open risk datasets, dashboards, an expert database, risk assessments and peer-reviewed papers. Its listed member organisations include the Indian Institute of Technology Roorkee, the University of Central Asia in Tajikistan, a research group in Pakistan, a mountain-hazards institute in China, a hydrological institute in Bhutan, and two regional agencies including the Aga Khan Agency for Habitat. Stated support comes from Geo Mountains and from the Glacier and Permafrost Hazards in Mountains standing group of the International Association of Cryospheric Sciences and the International Permafrost Association. Funding amounts and sources are not disclosed, no individuals are named, and the site is labelled beta. Cite it as a consortium finding attributed to the consortium; do not upgrade it to institutional authority.

open_threads.text: What standard of evidence the loss and damage fund applies to a claim from an event with no event-level attribution. The date fell and the answer is that there is no standard. The board allocated money on 22 October, and no public account of the decision text records any statement about what a claimant must show. D4 explains why that is not an oversight: a window declared one-time and country-specific needs no standard, because a standard is a thing a route has and there is no route. The question is therefore unchanged in substance and much sharper in form, and it has a new date — the December board meeting in the Philippines, which takes both the long-term model, including rapid disbursement, and the secretariat's commissioned assessment of the lessons of this one.

Whether any part of the deltacommissaris's ask — 1 per cent of national output to at least 2 — survives into a government commitment. Sixth checkpoint passed in silence. No cabinet response, no figure, nothing dated inside this week from any Dutch water institution on the financing question.

Whether an adaptation-limits argument is adjudicable by the institutions that will receive it. Tested this week for the first time, and the answer is that the institution adjudicated without engaging the argument. The fund that received the first disaster-specific claim in its history decided it by reference to the recovery cost and its own ceiling, not to the attribution study that found the event beyond existing risk reduction nor to the reconstruction that found the slope moving for seven weeks. So the argument was not rejected; it was unnecessary. That is a worse outcome for the claimant class than a rejection would have been, because an argument a decision does not need is an argument the next decision can also do without.

Who bears the privately held share of Nepal's losses, and whether a sovereign loss and damage claim can cover them. Advanced and narrowed. The fund has set aside 20 million dollars against a government recovery estimate of 4.8 billion, and 20 million is the fund's ceiling for a single project, so the answer to whether a sovereign claim can cover private loss is arithmetic: not at this ceiling, not at any plausible number of claims, and the question of who pays for the state-owned 341 MW hydropower project and the 759 MW of generation damaged in August is still entirely open. Nepal has been invited to submit a proposal; the proposal is the next document in which this could be addressed.

Whether any security institution reads the September sea-level declaration as a security instrument. Nothing, in a week with two venues where it could have been read that way and was not: the two Councils' joint seminar, whose five items do not mention it, and a conference presidency's allocation of five ministerial pairs, which includes an ocean pair with Palau on it and no mention of statehood continuity or maritime zones.

Whether the alliance's removal of the climate referent from its binding resilience baseline is a drafting choice or standing practice. The split answer of last week has not resolved and the confirming evidence has not arrived: the centre of excellence that uses the word freely on a programme page has published nothing from the meeting where it used it, so the evidence that the removal was drafting discipline rather than a change of mind still exists on a programme page and nowhere else.
Whether money reaches Somalia before the October-to-December rains.
open_threads.resolution: Answered yes, in part, and the answer required correcting this digest. Money did move before the rains: $7 million was pre-approved from the central emergency response fund in June for flood response preparedness ahead of the El Niño, alongside $10 million for drought response, and on 24 September Britain announced £5 million specifically for Deyr flood preparedness, split equally between a health, nutrition, water and protection programme led by Action Against Hunger and a Shabelle-basin rehabilitation programme delivered through three agencies, expected to reach about 600,000 people. Last week's digest said the money had not come; it had, one day before that was written. The proportions still carry the original finding: about £5 million and $7 million of anticipatory money against 2.5 to 3.5 million people exposed, roughly a million expected to be displaced, and a humanitarian plan at about a quarter funded. What happens next — whether the forecast verifies and whether the anticipatory money measurably reduced loss — is carried forward as a new question rather than as this one.

open_threads.text: Whether India or China responds to Nepal's proposal for a Himalayan Climate Resilience Mechanism, made from the General Assembly rostrum on 24 September. Fifth week, nothing from either capital. The week supplied a reason to keep asking: Nepal has now been invited to submit a proposal to the loss and damage fund, and a transboundary mechanism is one of the few things a 20 million dollar allocation could buy that the recovery itself cannot.

Whether the joint United Nations climate-security programme's third phase has a stated funding requirement, and whether contributions are rising, flat or falling. Unchanged and the route is still not taken: the consolidated annual and financial reports for 2025 remain unopened. What is new is a silence worth recording on its own — the unit's news stream's most recent items are from June and July. And a denominator: everything deposited to it from 2016 to 2024 comes to 18.27 million dollars, less than the single allocation the loss and damage fund made this week.

Whether the climate panel remains the reference science for climate decisions, on what timetable, and which states are pressing on each axis. Unchanged on the mechanism and sharpened on the consequence. Scientists have said they will continue drafting whatever the plenary decides, which separates the science from the certification; the certification is what instruments cite. The week's flagship emissions report shows what fills the space in the meantime — a programme report, not an assessed one, setting the numbers every delegation will quote at Antalya.

Whether any security institution treats the meteorological observing system's radio spectrum as an asset to be defended before the 2027 radiocommunication conference. Nothing new on spectrum. One adjacent movement: the director-general of a national meteorological institute now sits on a national security taskforce with a mandate to identify key risks to that country's security and resilience. That is the first time in this digest's run that someone responsible for an observing system has had a formal seat in a security-risk body, and it is the obvious place for the question to be asked. Whether it is asked there is checkable only if the taskforce publishes.

Whether any public institution produces an estimate of what Europe's 2026 heat season cost, to set against the private one. Unchanged, and the deadline is two days away. The only figure in circulation remains an insurer's — about 113 billion euros of annual output across thirty countries, roughly 0.46 per cent of combined projected output, from a proprietary model. If the Union's climate insurance alliance launches on 28 October without an independent basis for loss estimation, that figure becomes the official one by default.

Whether the Somali Deyr forecast verifies and whether the anticipatory money measurably reduced loss. The first half continues to verify and the second half now has numbers on both sides. The forecast held: above-normal rainfall is the regional outlook for the season and the Shabelle crossed its high flood-risk level on 13 October. The response: a projection of 874,319 people displaced between October and December, 92 per cent of it from flooding, against a preparedness requirement of 16.62 million dollars that is 14.4 per cent funded; Beletweyne and Gaalkacyo named as the most exposed, at roughly 229,000 and 82,000 people; the collective anticipatory framework and its triggers still unconfirmed as finalised; no district plans found, at a fourth checkpoint. The humanitarian chief has said the next two weeks are critical for this country, Ethiopia and Kenya. The measurement question that closes this thread — did the money reduce loss — will be answerable in the new year and nobody has said who will answer it.

Whether any candidate for Secretary-General states a position on climate, and in particular on Security Council competence over it. Nothing new this week; no straw poll, no candidate statement found. The Council's October closed with the succession as its most conspicuous business and no climate item in any framing, which is the context any eventual statement will be read against.
Whether the climate panel's plenary at Addis Ababa, 12 to 16 October, decides the timetable for its next assessment, and on which side.
open_threads.resolution: Answered, and the answer is neither of the two sides. The plenary did not decide. On the evening of Friday 16 October the chair, Jim Skea, suspended the session after it had run past its scheduled close and after delegations from least developed countries and small island developing states had left, rather than put the question to the room; the panel's statement says the timelines for the three working-group contributions and the panel's budget both "remain open" and that deliberations will resume "at the earliest opportunity", with no date given. Both subsidiary questions are answered the same way: the review of the panel's own principles and procedures was deferred for a further session, and nothing was decided about the budget, which is the item with a hard deadline because the 2027 budget depends on it and the panel must reconvene before the end of the year to set one. This was the sixth consecutive session to fail on the timetable, and the last scheduled before the November conference opens the second global stocktake's information phase. Around thirty countries pressed for all three reports by about September 2028; China, India, Kenya, Russia and Saudi Arabia are reported on the side of delivery in 2029 for the impacts and mitigation reports. The thread closes because its question had a date and the date has passed. Its successor is ipcc-resumed-session-budget, because the live question is no longer which side wins but whether the body can convene to decide at all.

open_threads.text: Whether the Union's reported position that there is no scope for new climate finance commitments at the November conference survives into adopted conclusions, and whether it holds at Antalya.
open_threads.resolution: The first half is answered and the answer is yes in substance and no in wording, which is the more interesting outcome. Environment ministers adopted the conclusions on 12 October as document 14250/26. The reported phrase does not appear. What appears instead is an absence: no new figure, no new instrument, no new pledge, a cross-reference to the separate climate finance conclusions approved by finance ministers on 9 October, a restatement of the New Collective Quantified Goal and the global goal of at least US$300 billion a year by 2035, support for at least tripling adaptation finance by 2035, and the record that developed countries provided and mobilised US$132.8 billion in 2023 and US$136.7 billion in 2024. A position that commits nothing does not have to say so. The second question — whether the extension of the mitigation work programme to at least 2040 was what the line was traded for — is answered in the negative and this digest had it wrong: the word 2040 does not appear anywhere in the adopted text, which asks only for the programme to be continued and strengthened. What was actually traded away was international carbon credits, removed from the innovative-finance list amid member-state disagreement about their place in the emissions trading system; only carbon pricing survives. The thread closes here rather than at Antalya because the mandate is now fixed and the conference will test it rather than the question. One sentence from the same document outlives the thread and is carried into section B instead: paragraph 7 calls climate change an existential threat to humanity, ecosystems and biodiversity "as well as to peace and security".

open_threads.text: Whether the 1996 Ganges treaty is renewed, replaced or allowed to lapse, and on what terms. Forty-eight days to expiry at the close of this week and nothing dated inside it. India's position, last stated on 9 October, is that the matter is handled within the Joint Rivers Commission; Bangladesh wants a new treaty with a guarantee clause on dry-season flow rather than a renewal and has a technical panel drafting its proposals. One factual discrepancy to settle before any of this is written up: the commission's meeting sequence is reported inconsistently — one brief gives an 86th meeting in March 2026 with three meetings a year, where this digest's roster has carried a 90th meeting in May 2026 — and the commission's own records are the only way to resolve it. The climate-stress framing of this renegotiation remains this publication's, not the literature's.
Whether anyone publishes how much anticipatory climate money has actually disbursed, as against pledged.
open_threads.resolution: Resolved against this digest. The figure exists and has been public since 28 May 2026, in the fourth annual global overview of anticipatory action produced by the Anticipation Hub with the UN food and agriculture agency, the UN humanitarian coordination office, the humanitarian start network, the food programme, the German Red Cross, the international federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent societies, their climate centre and a German development agency. For 2025: anticipatory action triggered 146 times across 54 countries, almost US$120 million released, 9.6 million people directly reached, 262 active frameworks against 154 the year before, a further 205 frameworks in development across 71 countries, and 57 countries described as institutionalising the approach; Germany and the European Union named as the largest contributors among donors who supplied data; money for acting before a hazard reported separately from money for building the systems. Three caveats travel with it and none of them restores the thread: "released" is the report's own verb and is self-reported by the implementing organisations, there is no independent audit or counterfactual, and there is no breakdown of how far ahead of impact the money actually moved. That last is the successor question and it is now carried as anticipatory-lead-time-figure. For the record of what the figure means: almost US$120 million worldwide in a year is about US$12.50 per person reached, and roughly nine thousandths of one per cent of the US$1.3 trillion a year by 2035 that the November conference will argue about.

open_threads.text: Whether solar radiation modification's arrival in government climate-security forums is a one-off or the start of an agenda. Unchanged. Nothing in the week from any government venue, and the institute that ran the Arctic tabletop published nothing on it. Its director's new appointment to a national taskforce is the thing to watch here: she is the person who took the security frame to this subject in the first place, and she now has a government seat.

Whether the Pacific Islands Forum's own climate fund reaches its 500 million dollar initial capitalisation target by the end of 2026. Nothing new inside this week. Worth reading alongside this week's pushback: the other fund in this field has received about 500 million dollars and has disbursed none of it, so a capitalisation target met is not a thing delivered, and whatever the Pacific fund reaches, the question that follows it is the route rather than the total.

Whether 1 million US dollars is the going rate for Dutch climate-security and climate-resilience money, or a floor the Netherlands happened to set at one venue. No new Dutch number this week. The comparison that has arrived instead is in kind rather than cash: the Netherlands supplied a national institute director to another government's security taskforce, which costs nothing and is worth more than the pledge.

Whether the climate panel reconvenes before the end of 2026, what it decides about its 2027 budget, and whether the budget and the assessment timetable are taken together. Nine days after the suspension there is still no date and no location. The secretariat's estimate for completing the cycle is about 33 million Swiss francs; the chair had proposed a 2027 budget similar to the indicative one considered at the sixty-third session and it was not agreed; the timeline scenarios were narrowed from seven to four without agreement, the dispute being whether the three working group contributions arrive in time for the second global stocktake in 2028 or slip to 2029. The panel has said it will resume at the earliest opportunity. The conference opens on 9 November.

Whether the forty-eight-day precursor signal on the slope above the Gyirong-Rasuwa corridor is treated as foreseeability by any institution that has to decide something. The first such institution decided on 22 October and did not treat it as anything: no public account of the loss and damage board's reasoning refers to the precursor reconstruction of 13 October or to the attribution study of 17 September. So the answer so far is that the question was available and nobody picked it up. The places it could still arrive: Nepal's own proposal to the fund, the secretariat's lessons assessment, any insurer or reinsurer pricing Himalayan hydropower, and any court anywhere. The moment one obligor asks what was measurable rather than what was attributable, every monitoring gap becomes a liability and every monitoring investment a defence.

Whether anyone publishes how far ahead of impact anticipatory money actually moves. Still nobody, and two new figures arrived this week that bear on the same hole from the financing side rather than the operational one. Cited by the director of a peace-research climate programme on 22 October, from a disaster-protection centre: about 1.2 per cent of development partners' crisis financing was pre-arranged in 2023, and fragile and conflict-affected settings received less than 7 per cent of international pre-arranged financing in 2024. Those are shares of a total rather than lead times, so the thread's question survives intact; they are recorded because they are the first numbers found that describe how much of the money is arranged in advance at all, and because they are somebody else's citation and have not been checked at source. Somalia remains the natural experiment: probabilities in August, river above its flood level on 13 October, appeal 14.4 per cent funded on the 21st.

Whether the first Dutch briefing on climate, nature and security is held during 2026, as a parliamentary motion asks. Nine weeks of the year left and nothing found. The contrast is now unavoidable and worth stating once: another European government held the first meeting of a standing ministerial body on exactly this subject on 21 October, with a Dutch institute director among its sixteen members, while the Dutch parliament's request for a single briefing has gone unanswered for seven months.

Whether the climate referent returns to a European Council conclusion in any substantive form. Nothing new; the October conclusions stand as the low-water mark. The next test is institutional rather than conciliar: whether the Commission's package of 28 October carries the referent into an instrument with money and a legal form, or into a framework of guidance. Reporting of the pre-briefing says there is no ring-fenced funding.

Whether the loss and damage fund's 20 million dollar ceiling for a single project and its out-of-cycle submission route become stated policy, and at what level. The ceiling is the binding constraint this week revealed: the first disaster-specific allocation in the fund's history was set at exactly the maximum the rules allow, which means the rules rather than the balance decided the number. The route was invented for one country and immediately described by three contributing governments as no precedent. The December board meeting in the Philippines takes the long-term model, including rapid disbursement, plus the secretariat's commissioned lessons assessment, plus the first project approvals. Three answerable questions there: is the ceiling raised or indexed to assessed loss, does the out-of-cycle route get written conditions, and does any document name an evidentiary standard.

Whether the projected tropical Pacific anomaly of up to 3.8°C for November to January verifies, and whether any security institution acts on the forecast before the peak. The meteorological agency has said the projection is off the monitoring scale it has used for four decades, which is a statement about its instrument as much as about the ocean. Two things are datable. The observed anomaly, which will be published monthly and settles whether the unprecedented language was right. And whether any defence ministry, alliance body or security council says anything at all about it before the end of the year — none has in five weeks of the forecast being public, and the humanitarian chief has put the critical window for Somalia, Ethiopia and Kenya at a fortnight from 21 October.

Whether the British climate and nature security taskforce produces anything, by when, and whether any of it reaches a spending document. Its published terms give it up to two meetings in 2026, one in person and one virtual, and an output described as an assessment of key gaps in the government's response, assurance of its strategic approach and recommendations for further work. No reporting date, no budget, no measurable target. That makes it the cheapest available form of taking this seriously and also the first standing national body of its kind, and the two readings are distinguished by one observable: whether a recommendation of its appears in a departmental spending or capability document. Secondary question with its own answer: whether a body with an American institute director, a Dutch meteorological chief and a German institute's security lead on it produces findings that are transferable to the countries they come from.

Whether "illegal exploitation of natural resources" becomes the Security Council's standing frame for resources and conflict. The 22 October seminar settled on that title after the African council proposed resource management and Russia proposed root causes, with European members resisting the Russian text; the United States and China co-led it. The frame matters because of what it admits and excludes: enforcement, sanctions and criminal networks are in; allocation, scarcity and climate stress are out. Datable answers: whether the title reappears in a Council product, whether any penholder tables a resolution or presidential statement using it, and whether the African Union's own council — which asked for the broader framing and has its own climate-security mandate, including a commissioned mapping of climate impacts in the Lake Chad basin and Sahel — restates the governance version in its own communiques.

Whether any government creates a body that is accountable for the gaps between its climate-security silos and gives it a budget line. This is the proposal put on 22 October by the director of the climate programme at the Swedish peace research institute, along with pre-agreed finance that releases when a forecast crosses a threshold. It is the clearest testable institutional proposition the field has produced this year, and this digest has been assembling the evidence for it from the other end for two months: an integrated Dutch strategy with 5 million euros and no action plan, an alliance resilience baseline with no named owner for its climate assumptions, a Somali forecast with no money attached to it. The answer will be visible in a budget document or not at all, and a taskforce with no budget — see the British one — is the thing most likely to be offered instead.

open_moves.text: Denmark's Security Council food-security debate, outcome document unconfirmed. Unchanged and October is nearly closed: the month's programme carries no food-security item in any framing and the only remaining route is the joint seminar with the African Union on 21 and 22 October, where the framing would be the African Union's to bring. Worth noting against it that a famine risk was classified in Somalia this month and no Council member raised it.

The American climate-security institute's philanthropic-funding bet. Fourth consecutive week of movement in the same direction and the register has now changed completely. The week's one new item is an event announcement for 27 October, "Charging Forward: Electric Vehicles as Defense Technology", moderated by the institute's own director, arguing that advanced batteries are a chokepoint technology on a par with semiconductors, that China dominates the supply chain, and that without a domestic electric-vehicle market the United States risks ceding a technology central to its future military capability. No climate content in the framing; no climate research published; a fourth week without a state-level briefer; the parent's new fellowship on artificial intelligence and national security closing applications on 20 October. This is a serious argument in the register that is currently funded, and it is not this field.

The Abyei climate, peace and security report and the next peacekeeping mandate renewal. Unchanged. The Stockholm institute's climate-change-and-security publications list still ends at the August Abyei study with nothing for September or October, which under this digest's split rule is lead time from a research institute and not a finding. Four mandate renewals fall on 31 October and the Council's Africa items in late October remain where this resolves.
PIF security-declaration merger.

The Union's climate resilience framework, announced in the State of the Union address of 16 September. Now reported for 28 October, with a European heatwave plan, a water initiative and a climate insurance alliance alongside it. Reporting of the pre-briefing describes a hundred most-vulnerable territories, named risk owners across sectors, a 3°C reference scenario for infrastructure investment and no ring-fenced money, with adaptation tied to the long-term budget negotiation; none of that is confirmed against a Commission document. Two days from an answer.

Succession to the Secretary-General. Advanced and still unresolved. A sixth straw poll on 16 October, the first with colour-coded ballots separating the five permanent members from the ten elected, with China and the United States as tellers: the leader on nine encourage and five discourage but opposed by two permanent members, two others on eight encourage and six discourage and also opposed by two, one discouraged by all five. Nobody withdrew, nobody new entered, and an analyst's reading is "a split decision with no P5 convergence". A regional claim entered on 13 October from the Latin American and Caribbean group. The incumbent's term ends on 31 December. For this field the finding is unchanged through six polls: no candidate has been asked a public question about climate or about Council competence over it. Recorded separately as this week's D5, because the colour-coding is itself a move.

The Turkish presidency of the Antalya conference, 9 to 20 November, with Australia running the negotiations. Advanced on the negotiations side: five ministerial pairs named on 20 October for mitigation, adaptation, finance, just transition and ocean, with no pair for loss and damage and none for anything security-framed. The second global stocktake begins at the conference.

Whether overshoot is adopted as a planning premise by security institutions or stays inside the climate-policy system. Advanced quietly and in the Union's own adopted text: the conclusions of 12 October reiterate the aim of "bringing the temperature increase to or below 1.5C by the end of the century", which is overshoot language adopted as a negotiating position without being described as such, drawing on the UN environment programme's report of 2 October. No security institution has adopted the premise, which is the original question and still unanswered.
open_moves.resolution: Completed, and promoted. What was a spotlight report on limiting overshoot on 2 September is now the headline of the programme's flagship pre-conference document: the Emissions Gap Report 2026, subtitled The Point of Return, treats exceeding 1.5°C as virtually unavoidable and reframes the objective as minimising the peak and the duration and returning below the limit by 2100. The move landed. What it did not carry with it is any treatment of adaptation, adaptation limits, loss and damage or security, in any of the published readings.

open_moves.text: The small island states' refusal of the overshoot frame, published within a day of the programme's September spotlight report. Not restated when the same concession became the flagship: no statement on the Emissions Gap Report of 21 October as of the 25th, with the group's statements page ending at 5 October. Either the position is being held in reserve for Antalya or the refusal has run out of places to be made.

Whether the pre-event-indications finding produces a funded glacier-hazard early-warning programme, and whether it can survive the China-Nepal data wall. Advanced sharply and from an unexpected quarter. The mountain centre's reconstruction of 13 October supplies the strongest pre-event indication yet found for any event in this digest's run — up to 40 cm of satellite-measured slope movement over forty-eight days — and recommends integrating satellite, seismic and hydrological monitoring with impact-based forecasting and cross-border information sharing. On the data wall, the one encouraging observable: a joint field mission with the centre's China office began this week on both sides of the border. Against that, the bilateral mechanism that would have to carry a state-level data question is two months past a commitment to meet, and Nepal's regional proposal is four weeks unanswered. Still no funding.

Whether Nepal's restriction of foreign search-and-rescue becomes a precedent or an episode. Superseded and closing next week unless something revives it. Nepal's posture is outward-facing in every direction: a sovereign claim about to receive the first disaster-specific decision in the loss and damage fund's history, a regional mechanism proposed from the Assembly rostrum, and a joint cross-border scientific mission under way.

Whether the climate convention secretariat's economic-security framing is picked up outside the climate-policy system, and in particular whether any European security institution adopts the formulation.
open_moves.resolution: Answered on both halves and not in the way the question expected. A European security institution did adopt a security framing: on 24 September the Union's High Representative for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy co-hosted a foreign ministers' dialogue on climate change and ecosystem degradation as national security risks. But it adopted this field's own formulation, national security risk, not the secretariat's economic-security substitution. And the secretary himself substituted again in the same week, telling Climate Week that electrification shields countries, families and businesses from fossil-fuel supply shocks and calling it a development strategy, an industrial strategy, a health strategy and a security strategy — security fourth, and meaning supply security. So the two moved past each other: the institution reached for the field's register in the same week the secretariat reached past it. The question is closed because its premise has been falsified. It assumed the secretariat's phrasing would be the vector by which the security frame travelled into European institutions, and the frame travelled without it.

open_moves.text: Whether the deltacommissaris's two-per-cent ask converts into any government commitment. Fifth checkpoint passed with silence: no cabinet response to the 2027 programme and nothing on water in the responsible committee, in a week when the chamber was sitting. The nearest pressure remains external and is now ten days off — the European framework of 28 October and its expected requirement of named risk owners, which is awkward for a governance model built on distributed responsibility.

Nepal's claim on the loss and damage fund for the August cascade. Advanced and capped. The board set aside 20 million dollars on 22 October against a government recovery estimate of 4.8 billion, and invited a proposal; nothing has been disbursed and no payment timeline has been given. The next document is Nepal's own proposal, and the next date is the December board in the Philippines, where the first project approvals are expected.
Whether the rescission was announced as expected, whether the endangerment-finding proposal followed, and whether the Houston ministerial's outcome document mentions climate.
open_moves.resolution: All three answered. The partial repeal of the carbon pollution standards for fossil-fuel-fired power plants was finalised on 14 September 2026 by Administrator Lee Zeldin, signed at the G20 Energy Abundance Ministerial in Houston rather than on its sidelines; the agency prices it at $310 billion in savings and calls it the largest power-sector deregulatory action in US history. The separate proposal followed simultaneously: EPA proposed rescinding every remaining greenhouse-gas standard for the sector, the vehicle for repealing the power-plant endangerment finding, with $370 million in claimed direct compliance-cost savings. And the ministerial's outcome document, a Critical Minerals Meeting Communiqué, does not mention climate: it grounds critical minerals in energy security, digital infrastructure, emerging technologies and economic development, and calls for voluntary and collaborative cooperation respecting national sovereignty and 'different domestic pathways'. Canada's own readout of the meeting likewise contains no reference to climate change. Environmental organisations have said they will litigate. The substitution this digest read off the ministerial's branding last week is confirmed in a negotiated multilateral text, which is why this closes as landed rather than as too early.

open_moves.text: Whether the alliance ever states what happened to the Secretary-General's annual climate and security assessment. Still no statement, and the displacing event has now been held: the centre of excellence's Montreal summit of 15 and 16 October, by invitation, on how to invest the climate-relevant share of a rising defence budget. The centre has published nothing about it as of 19 October, against recaps of the 2024 and 2025 editions within days of each. Recorded as this week's D4.

Whether the relocation of the evidentiary question from causation to adaptation limits is taken up by the institutions that have to apply it. The most consequential week yet and the news is not what the move expected. No fund board, bank, insurer or court has reasoned from adaptation limits, five weeks on. What happened instead is that the premise acquired a counter-argument from the research side: the mountain centre's reconstruction of 13 October finds a forty-eight-day measurable precursor on the slope, against the attribution network's conclusion that no early warning system could have given sufficient lead time. The network itself published this week on a Pacific hurricane and nothing on the Horn of Africa or on Europe's heat season. The first institution that must choose between the two framings is the fund board on 22 October.
Whether the American climate-security field's move to the state level is a durable relocation or a holding pattern.
open_moves.resolution: Answered no, and closed. Four consecutive weeks with no new state-level briefer since Ohio on 18 September; no state government named as commissioner or partner on any of the five; no second American institute writing for statehouses; and the institute's new programme capacity going elsewhere twice over — the parent's fellowship on artificial intelligence and national security, applications closing 20 October, and the institute's own event of 27 October on electric vehicles as defence technology. The statehouse series was one bet among several and it is not the one being pressed. The successor question is not where American climate-security work relocates geographically but which register it survives in, and on this month's evidence the answer is technology and supply-chain competition with China. That is carried by the csr-ccs-staffing move rather than as a new thread.

open_moves.text: Whether the asymmetry in the Dutch budget — flood defence funded, spatial adaptation and freshwater reduced over the longer term — survives the cabinet's response to the 2027 delta programme and the autumn estimates. No amendment and no cabinet response found; the parliamentary budget rounds on infrastructure and water fall later in the autumn, so this is still lead time. The defence side hardened again: the EUR 5 million structural climate-security line stands and the action plan that would spend it is three months and fifteen days overdue. One new instrument on the same lane, from March and not from this week: a motion asking the government to hold a first national briefing on climate, nature and security during 2026, whose adoption could not be confirmed.

The British, European and Kenyan foreign ministers' dialogue on climate change and ecosystem degradation as national security risks, 24 September. Four weeks on, no institutional follow-through from any of the three and nothing from the Union's external action service. What the Union did produce in the same period is a Council mandate naming climate change a threat to peace and security with no security institution mentioned anywhere in it — the formulation travelled into a text and not into any machinery. The service's climate envoy appears on the Montreal summit speaker list, in a role title no European source confirms.

The British climate security package of September 2026. Advanced in a form this move did not anticipate: on 21 October the energy security department published the sixteen-member membership of a National Security and Resilience Risks of a Changing Climate and Nature Loss Taskforce and held its first meeting, co-chaired by the Minister for Climate Transition. The package has produced an institution rather than only money, and the institution has no budget. See D1.

Nepal's proposal, from the General Assembly rostrum on 24 September, for a Himalayan Climate Resilience Mechanism led by Nepal, India and China. Fourth week, no response from either capital, and this week the silence acquired an explanation that is not about either capital's disposition: an Indian institute's report with a Dutch partner argues that regional climate proposals in South Asia get designed for political feasibility rather than for the risk, and that sovereignty and information-sharing sensitivities shape what can be proposed at all. On that reading an unanswered proposal is the system working as it does. The one thing that did cross the border this week was a joint technical field mission.

The alliance's revision and first public release of its seven baseline requirements for resilience, 15 September. Nothing new from the alliance, and the test of whether the climate referent's removal was a drafting discipline returned a split answer: the centre of excellence's Montreal summit named climate throughout its own programme, which is the pattern predicted, but the centre published nothing from it, so the free use of the word exists on a programme page and nowhere else. The same operation has now been performed at Union level by the European Council, where neither the climate referent nor any hazard referent appears in the resilience and preparedness language.

Australia's Climate Week keynote on climate security as national security, 21 September, and the challenge to it from a former chief of defence asking where the plan is. Nothing new. Australia holds the presidency of negotiations at Antalya and the Union's adopted mandate is now the text its negotiators will meet; nothing Australian and security-framed was found inside the week. Keynote and chairmanship remain separate registers for the same minister.

Fiji's four-pillar position for the pre-conference talks, set out on 29 September. One arithmetic refinement from the pledging round: Tonga's prime minister said the region still needs US$320 million, which against the US$500 million target implies about US$180 million raised rather than the about US$190 million this digest carried. The science pillar remains untransacted and this week shows why in the sharpest possible form — the decision it was aimed at was taken, or rather not taken, in a scientific-governance plenary where the Pacific's position was carried by the Marshall Islands and the outcome was a suspension.

The American climate-security institute's private tabletop on the security dynamics of a fictional 2030 stratospheric aerosol deployment, 14 October. No acknowledgement, no output and no participants named, as expected — but the framing this digest attached to it was wrong and is corrected. The same institute published in February 2026, from an earlier exercise in the same series, a named-author report with a specified scenario and a named technical partner that built the simulator: 3 teragrams of sulphur dioxide a year over the Arctic at 60 degrees north from 2035 to 2040, rising to a global peak of 14 by 2100, against SSP2-4.5, from a tabletop at New York Climate Week in September 2025 with more than twenty-five foreign and security policy experts and no team playing the United States. So the format does produce a record; what it withholds is who was in the room. Its conclusions are the thing to watch for adoption: that states will default to geopolitical instinct rather than to science, that Russia is the central risk including disinformation framing the consortium as neo-colonial, that China may oppose publicly while benefiting privately, and that a trusted multilateral assessment is the precondition for any of it.

Greece's Security Council programme of work for October, announced 1 October. Two-thirds through the month and the finding holds: no climate, water, food-security or environment item in any framing. What the presidency has run instead is the succession, including the first colour-coded straw poll in the process's history on 16 October. The joint seminar with the African Union on 21 and 22 October is the only remaining route and the month closes on 31 October with four mandate renewals.

The Berlin climate and security conference of 6 October, hosted by the German foreign ministry with the institute that founded it. Open on the only question the format leaves — whether any defence ministry repeats the weaponisation claim — and nothing this week repeated it. One adjacent observable: the alliance's climate centre attended the 2025 Berlin conference and published a note about it on 23 October 2025; no equivalent note has appeared for 2026, which is consistent with a centre that currently publishes almost nothing rather than with a changed relationship.

The presidency's pricing of the climate finance ask against the alliance's defence commitment, made at the Nadi pre-conference talks on 8 October. Nobody has taken the comparison up on either side this week. The counter-move this digest predicted — that climate money should come out of the 1.5 points of defence-related spending — was the subject of an invitation-only summit on 15 and 16 October that has published nothing, so the comparison is live and unrecorded in both directions.
The Union's draft negotiating position for the November conference, reported on 6 October from a copy seen by a financial wire, stating there is no scope for new climate finance commitments.
open_moves.resolution: Landed, in substance and not in wording. The conclusions were adopted by environment ministers in Luxembourg on 12 October as document 14250/26 under the Irish presidency, chaired by climate minister Darragh O'Brien. The reported phrase is not in the text; what is in the text is an absence of any new commitment, a cross-reference to the separate climate finance conclusions of 9 October, and a restatement of existing goals. The expected trade did not happen: the word 2040 appears nowhere, and the mitigation work programme is only to be continued and strengthened. What was traded away was international carbon credits, deleted from the innovative-finance list; only carbon pricing survives. Two things from the same document outlive this move and are carried forward instead. Its paragraph 7 calls climate change an existential threat to humanity, ecosystems and biodiversity "as well as to peace and security". And its paragraph 11 condemns Russia's war of aggression and reiterates concern about the Middle East, in the strategic framing of a climate mandate, with nothing joining either to anything climatic — which is the current limit of what the Union will assert, in a text revised five times.

open_moves.text: The loss and damage fund's board called the first extraordinary meeting in its existence, for 22 October, on a draft decision provisionally setting aside US$20 million for Nepal and piloting a route for requests outside the fund's regular call for proposals.
open_moves.resolution: Held and decided. The board agreed unanimously to set aside 20 million dollars for Nepal plus 1.6 million in administrative and oversight fees — which settles last week's small question: the fees sit on top of the allocation, not inside it — and invited Nepal to submit a proposal for a later meeting. Nothing has been disbursed. The out-of-cycle route was used and then disowned as a precedent by three contributing governments; see D4. The decision text, by the only account that read it, says nothing about the standard of evidence a claim from an unattributed event must meet.

open_moves.text: The panel's chair suspended the sixty-fifth plenary on 16 October rather than decide without the delegations that had gone home, leaving the assessment timetable and the 2027 budget open. Nine days later there is still no resumption date and no location, against a requirement to reconvene before the year ends to adopt a budget at all. Scientists have said they will keep drafting regardless, which preserves the science and not the certification.

An Indian institute's workshop report with a Dutch partner, published 12 October as Special Report 227, arguing that shared climate vulnerability in South Asia does not produce collective action because governance is national and siloed, sovereignty and information-sharing sensitivities constrain what can be proposed, and asymmetries make states facing one hazard set different priorities. Open on whether its nine observations are picked up by anyone designing a regional mechanism — Nepal's proposal being the live candidate — and on whether any Indian or Chinese official engages the argument.

The alliance's climate centre convened the Montréal climate security summit on 15 and 16 October, by invitation, on how to spend the climate-relevant share of a rising defence budget. Ten days on, neither host has published anything about it, against recaps within days of both previous editions and a Canadian defence minister's speech published on his own government's site for the 2025 edition. See D5: the comparison has moved this from a silence to a contrast.

The Security Council's first use of colour-coded ballots in a straw poll on the succession, on 16 October, separating the five permanent members from the ten elected so that a potential veto is visible without being attributable. Open on whether a seventh poll is held before the end of the year, whether colour-coding is retained, and — the only question that matters here — whether anyone asks any candidate a public question about climate or about Council competence over it before the choice is made.

A British department published the membership of the first standing ministerial climate and nature security taskforce and held its inaugural meeting: sixteen members, among them an American institute director, the Dutch national meteorological institute's director-general and a German institute's climate diplomacy and security lead; up to two meetings in 2026; no reporting date, no budget, no measurable target. Open until it publishes something or a recommendation of its appears in a spending document.

The director of the Swedish peace research institute's climate programme argued that climate security's problem is ownership rather than coordination, attacked the threat-multiplier formulation as naming no mechanism, and proposed one accountable central body with a budget line plus pre-agreed finance released on forecast thresholds. Open until any government adopts or rejects the proposition, or until the formulation he attacked is dropped from an alliance or Union document.

The conference's president of negotiations named five ministerial pairs to facilitate mitigation, adaptation, finance, just transition and ocean, three weeks before the conference. No pair for loss and damage. Open until the conference shows whether the absent file was left to the fund's board by design or by omission.

Germany, Czechia and Japan placed on the record that the fund's first allocation sets no precedent and is truly exceptional, against Pakistan's and Ecuador's attempts to make it learnable; the board did commission a lessons assessment from its secretariat. Open until the December board either writes conditions for the out-of-cycle route or confirms that there is none.

housekeeping:
**What could not be read this week, and what it costs you.**

The environment programme's own pages for the Emissions Gap Report refused retrieval, as did its press release and its document repository. Every figure in B4 therefore comes from the UN's news service and from the fullest independent reading of the report published the same day, which agree with each other on all the numbers used. Two consequences: a carbon-removal volume attributed to the report by one secondary outlet is not reported here, and the claim that the launch took place in London rather than Nairobi is not reported either.

The British Defence Committee's own text would not open from any route tried, including the parliamentary publication and the committee's own file. B6 therefore rests on three independent published accounts, which agree closely on the capability findings and on the climate premise. What that costs you is specific: it is not established whether any of the report's formal conclusions and recommendations names climate change, and the item says so rather than implying an absence.

The African Union's adopted communique from the 21 October peacebuilding meeting, and the Security Council's own press record for the 23rd, both failed to load. So B5 reports what the two Councils scheduled and what they argued about the title, from an independent monitoring organisation's pre-meeting accounts, and not what they said in the room.

The Dutch flagship platform's own site refused for a seventh consecutive week, which means the Netherlands entry in section C records a hole in the observation and not a finding about that institute.

Against all that, one thing worked. The curriculum item in A1 was read in full — the whole twenty-four pages — from a university research group's archived scan, after the publisher refused. That is the second time the same route has opened a canonical article in this sequence, and it is the reason this week's section A quotes the author's own words instead of summarising summaries. The recent item in A2 is open-licence and was read in full as well. For the first time in four weeks, nothing in section A rests on an abstract.

**Corrections to the published record.** Two. Last week this publication left open whether the Nepal allocation was 20 million dollars or 21.6; it is 20 million of recovery assistance with 1.6 million of oversight fees on top. And this publication has for several weeks framed the loss and damage fund's difficulty as a shortage of capital; the correction is in the *Pushback* section above, because it is an argument rather than an erratum.

**Length.** Longer than usual, because four of the week's items were decisions rather than events and decisions have to be quoted to be checkable.
